entities.name: Merriam-Webster
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Merriam-Webster, founded in 1831 in Springfield, Massachusetts, serves as a cornerstone of American lexicography and education. Established by George and Charles Merriam, along with their partner, Edward A. Webster, the company arose during a transformative period in the United States characterized by rapid linguistic evolution and burgeoning nationalism. The publishing house's commitment to standardizing and defining American English has made it a notable institution in the realm of language and education across North America, facilitating clearer communication in an increasingly diverse society.

The company initially gained prominence with the publication of its first dictionary, 'An American Dictionary of the English Language' in 1836, authored by Noah Webster, an early American lexicographer whose work was pivotal in distinguishing American English from British English. This dictionary was revolutionary, boasting over 70,000 entries, and established a new standard for American language, promoting a sense of national identity. Merriam-Webster’s dictionaries evolved through the 19th and 20th centuries, incorporating new words and adapting to changes in society, such as the inclusion of terms reflecting technological advancements and cultural shifts.

The legacy of Merriam-Webster extends beyond mere word definitions; it has influenced educational curricula and language policies in the United States, reinforcing the importance of a standardized language for effective governance and social cohesion. As a reference tool, its dictionaries have been integral to the educational foundation of millions, shaping literacy and communication. Additionally, the company's adaptation to digital formats and online resources has ensured its relevance in the 21st century, continuing to serve as a vital resource for language learners and scholars alike.
